cells.tense: You are here in the middle of it, and endings are arriving on their own schedule.
cells.act: let an exchange flow both ways
cells.ask: Between you and someone, a favour or a running tab has been kept square. Let it drift this week without tracking the return. No clock on it. Set the ledger down and see.
cells.core:
Something in your life is already finishing, and you can feel that it is. You're not fighting it and you're not rushing it — you're letting it take the time it takes, and you're still around while it does. That's rarer than it sounds, and it's what makes the next thing possible rather than just hoped for.

When a thing ends, you don't need to know what fills the space. The clearing is the point. So let one exchange go loose. There's a place between you and someone where you've kept the books even — a favour given, a favour owed. Drop it for now. Not forever, not as a rule. Long enough to feel what happens when you're not holding the scale. Fairness that flows finds its own level without a hand on it. That's the part you're trusting, and you can afford to.
cells.sheetLine: You let things finish, and you stay around while they do.
cells.verb: ending what's done so what's next can start
cells.place: the doorway you keep half-open behind you

cells.tense: You will be braced for the next thing to end before it has even begun to live.
cells.act: stay in contact while it is hard
cells.ask: Next time you feel the pull to end something early — a plan, a project, a tie — don't decide yet. Stay near it through one more hard stretch. Not fixing it. Just not gone from it.
cells.core:
You're ending things ahead of their time. Not because they're finished, but because finishing them early feels like freedom, and waiting feels like a trap. It isn't. The upheaval looks like liberation from the outside and feels like bracing from where you sit — you're already three endings past where you actually are.

Courage isn't the gap. Company is. Something is being carried near you — a person, a situation, a piece of work — and you're managing it from a distance instead of standing next to it. Stay close through the hard part. Not fixing, not deciding, not ending. Just staying. The true ending will still be there when it's true. The ones you jump to now are the ones you'll be finishing again later, and twice is worse than once.
cells.sheetLine: You're ending things before they've had a chance to be.
cells.verb: ending what's done so what's next can start
cells.place: the doorway you keep half-open behind you

cells.tense: You were still at a door that closed behind you a long while ago.
cells.act: go where the feeling is already pulling
cells.ask: Something you want is already pulling at you. Follow it one step today, in the direction your body already leans. No plan, no permission, no announcement to anyone.
cells.core:
Something in your life finished a while back and you've kept it standing. You tell yourself it's loyalty, or patience, or being the kind of person who doesn't walk away. It might be all of those. It's also a weight you're carrying because putting it down would mean it really ended, and ending is the thing you've been avoiding for longer than you'd say plainly.

The way out isn't a bigger push. It's a smaller one, in a direction you already have. There's something you want that you haven't moved toward — not a project, just a pull. Go where that pull is, one step, today. You don't need to feel ready. You don't need to know what you're releasing. The movement does the clearing. Holding still doesn't hold anything; it keeps you in a room you already left.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding something up that already finished its life.
cells.verb: ending what's done so what's next can start
cells.place: the doorway you keep half-open behind you

cells.tense: Something is ending in you right now, and you have no words for it yet.
cells.act: put a date, a place, a container on it
cells.ask: Take whatever has been taking up room — a plan, a habit, a commitment — and give it edges: a date it's done, a place it stops. Once it has a shape, leave it be.
cells.core:
You can't name what's shifting. Something in you is letting go and the part of you that writes things down hasn't caught up. You'll feel it as fog, or flatness, or a low hum of something you can't place — and you'll treat it as a problem to solve rather than a change already underway.

You don't have to know what it is. Give it a container anyway. Take whatever has been taking up room — a plan, a habit, a commitment you keep half-holding — and put an edge on it: a date it's done, a place it stops. The shape makes it visible. Visible, you can work with it. The ending was going to happen whether or not you named it. Naming it just means you get to be there for it.
cells.sheetLine: Something is ending in you, and you haven't met it yet.
cells.verb: ending what's done so what's next can start
cells.place: the doorway you keep half-open behind you

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person can name what is ending, or feel necessity, from the inside — the record only says this capacity is present, not that they have words for it. The reader could reasonably say 'I'm not holding on, I just haven't decided yet,' and the Too Little read would need to bend. The ask survives being wrong because releasing a calendar half-hour is useful whether or not the diagnosis lands, and nothing in it depends on the person agreeing with me. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line that makes the release sound noble rather than simply done, so I keep the location and drop the praise.
